speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, That the total sum to be allocated for Head W of the Estimates be reduced by $100.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our hearts, sympathies and thoughts go out to their respective families in their grief during this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is especially so, as MOT embarks on a comprehensive and ambitious plan to achieve the vision of providing Singaporeans with a modern, state-of-the-art, efficient and effective public transport system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As we set out to achieve this, we should be mindful that necessary safety precautions and protocols are considered and implemented in tandem.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must ensure that all safety protocols are followed and strictly adhered to.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If there is a lapse in any way or form, immediate corrective measures must be taken with utmost priority.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Only then, can we have a 21st century public transport system we can truly be proud of.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the accident remains the subject of investigations, I shall not comment on it any further.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As I alluded to earlier, MOT has a comprehensive and ambitious plan to transform Singapore's transportation sector.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A quick look at key upcoming projects reveals the reason why.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Terminal 5 and our third runway are off the mark.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Walk Cycle Ride SG initiative and the proposed North-South Corridor for commuters, cyclists and pedestrians will change the transportation lifestyle mindset of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Amid this backdrop, however, is also the Land Transport Authority’s (LTA) and Intelligent Transportation Society Singapore's (ITSS) Smart Mobility 2030, which maps out Singapore's Intelligent Transport System Strategic Plan.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The plan is to leverage technological advances to improve connectivity and efficiency in our transport system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Locally, Singapore is restricted by its physical size.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The demographic and size of our population are changing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a new emphasis on green technology which includes vehicles with less carbon emissions, hybrid and electric cars, even driverless cars.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I spoke earlier of the dichotomy of being efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Being effective, however, is about doing the right things.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We plan, execute and implement projects and plans exceedingly well.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But let us pause and consider if we do it in an effective way.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: First, are Singaporeans adequately prepared to accept this changing transportation model?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The ownership of cars is a norm in many countries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our population has grown significantly over the years and we expect it to grow more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Similarly, the number of vehicles has also grown.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have tried with land reclamation but we are clearly limited by what we can do.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The transport infrastructure model that is before us is clearly an efficient solution to this problem.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It makes the best use of what we have, the best use of what modern technology can give us and plan it in the best way we know how.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But to make this transport infrastructure model also the most effective solution, the population that lives in this model must also participate actively and make the best use of it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is an issue close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In Potong Pasir, a significant proportion of my residents are elderly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The elderly are physically more constrained than the young.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As such, we must be sensitive and aware of their travel needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a new housing development now being built in Potong Pasir.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The land it is on is directly next to Potong Pasir MRT station.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: During construction, the developer blocked off the most direct walking route that my residents take to the MRT station.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The developer was required to build sheltered walkways along the perimeter of the land to facilitate our residents' needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Yes, sheltered walkways are good but it is now a more circuitous route.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For a young adult or even a not-so-young adult like me, we can manage.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But for an elderly person, this extra 10 minutes of walking can be a torturous and excruciating exercise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is exactly the type of programme we need to make our transportation model a successful one.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Reliability of our public transport system, especially of our MRT system, has been an issue raised on many occasions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But with the rapid expansion of the MRT lines or of a new line or extension every year for the next five years, is this a case of biting off more than we can chew?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Are we equipped to ensure reliability across the entire MRT system while expanding its capacity at the same time?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: MOT has an impressive plan and is building a transportation model to facilitate and allow more Singaporeans to do so.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as we efficiently go about planning and implementing this model, we should keep in mind other factors that could affect the ultimate effectiveness of the model.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite Minister to share with us any of the Ministry's current and/or future plans to address these issues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, the expansion of the MRT network in recent years has brought about many spanking and beautifully designed stations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These stations are spacious and brightly lit with futuristic designs and decorated with artwork.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of the larger stations house a generous array of shops and eateries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the overcrowding at the platform be resolved?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it shield my residents from the hot morning sun?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it cover my residents' bicycles from rain and shine?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be more elderly-friendly with the provision of more seats, brighter and bigger signages?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be beautiful artwork displays perhaps to cool them down when they cannot squeeze into the overcrowded train and have to wait for the next train?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be more friendly for handicapped residents, especially the visually handicapped?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps numbering of bays with protruded numbers or letters will help tremendously.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure my favourite compassionate and Mr-Fix-It Minister will help us.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years ago at the COS debates, my colleague, Mr Png Eng Huat, spoke about the reliability of our train services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years on, the regularity of train disruptions, the reliability of our MRT system remains a disconcerting issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most recent major one was a four-hour disruption on the East-West Line on 19 March.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just last Friday, there was another train fault on the Circle Line.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In December 2015, LTA started a new method of measuring service delay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last week, LTA reported that the average distance clocked between overall breakdowns had increased.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was cited as a statistic for rail reliability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Straits Times article of 7 April stated that "it is hard for anyone to reconcile an improvement in reliability when major breakdowns have spiked".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, whatever statistics that LTA may use, commuters who use the MRT everyday can attest for themselves the frequency of disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans should not have to get used to this regularity of disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We expect our system to have far fewer disruptions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also be greatly concerned with the loss of productivity to all our workers and our economy arising from the man-hours lost to all delays over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Several Members in this House, including Minister Khaw Boon Wan, Minister Yaacob Ibrahim and Minister Masagos Zulkifli have visited the families to extend their condolences.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many questions popped up in my mind when I heard about the incident.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can a train hit the two staff who were walking in the second and third position in a single file on a designated walkway?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do we need 15 people on the tracks?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is it right to put trainees on the track during train operating hours?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is safety compromised because SMRT is pushing for shorter downtime?" Over the next few days after the tragic accident, further details emerged and more questions came to mind, "Why was the initial account of the incident different?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we expect our maintenance crew to do a good job if they think their lives might be in danger?" Chairman, for a system that runs on tracks, it is not acceptable to have any serious injury, especially fatal ones.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such incidents not only undermine public confidence in our train operators, but I am sure it would have deeply affected staff morale at SMRT and also affect its attractiveness as an employer for people looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that SMRT has completed its internal investigations into this incident and the report is being reviewed by an independent panel.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hopefully, this will answer the many questions which I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also hope MOT will look into whether financial or other penalties should be imposed on SMRT and its management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am surprised that such a simple accident can be allowed to happen here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Not all reputable MRT operators in the world allow workers to effect repairs on maintenance on tracks while trains are in operation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: On the morning of 30 March, I filed my present COS cut on Safety Protocols for MRT Operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I had expected these measures to be in place and to be the so-called standard operating procedures (SOPs).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If they were, the press release would not have been necessary.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the developments in transport and its associate technology have been rapid in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just last week, NuTonomy, a driverless car startup out of the US sets its sights on operating a fully autonomous taxi service out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The future of transport is arriving on our shores and sooner than we realise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The difference in views between LTA and car manufacturer Tesla on test methodology for its cars earlier this year gained widespread international attention.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The incident exemplifies this need for us to be ready to master new developments quickly and continuously engage new technology manufacturers to ensure that our laws, regulations and methods are up to date.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In terms of public transportation, what other developments can Singaporeans expect and how will these trends encourage greater use, provide greater confidence as well as real-time information and enhance the reliability of our own public transport system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The recent announcement of Electronic Road Pricing 2.0 (ERP2) is certainly a game changer and I am keen to know the Ministry's plans to balance the pace of transition in adopting this new technology.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the rapid pace of adoption, it is especially important for the Ministry to guide Singaporeans through these investments and developments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Ministry consults the public widely on the policy changes and inform them in advance of impending changes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In a press release by LTA last October, autonomous vehicles are touted to radically transform our land transportation, especially in two key areas of constraint − land and manpower.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Committee on Autonomous Road Transport (CARTS) in Singapore was reported to be looking into some key roles for autonomous vehicles to complement our transport system in the hope of reducing road congestion during peak hours and manpower requirements.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While I am not sure how autonomous vehicles can help Singapore ease its constraint on land use, the technology can certainly ease the manpower crunch in the public transport arena.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I do see the potential for autonomous vehicle to complement our public transport system, especially in the area of feeder bus service where the route is short and fixed and standard fare applies.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I do see the potential for autonomous feeder bus service to take over from one-man-operated (OMO) bus service at night when the traffic is light and to stay operational longer as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the same vein, transport by CARTS, there was no mention of allowing private autonomous vehicles on our road.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Innovative technologies, such as induction charging, can further boost capacity.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These batteries are also made in increasingly environmentally friendly ways with chemical materials in the batteries capable of being recycled.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Zero tail pipe emissions also mean that electric buses provide public transportation which is cleaner and quieter.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the upfront costs are currently higher, there is growing evidence that the lifecycle costs are becoming increasingly more competitive.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister if he would consider using electric buses for our public transport system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our public bus captains carry a heavy responsibility every day when they report for work, because thousands of commuters depend on public buses to safely and promptly reach their destinations all over Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the introduction of the Bus Service Enhancement Programme (BSEP) and the Bus Service Reliability Framework (BSRF), as well as the implementation of the Government Contracting Model (GCM), more bus captains are required in the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, to make the Omnibus Driver Vocational Licence (ODVL) transferable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bus captains currently possess this vocational licence, valid only while the holder is a bus driver with Singapore Bus Service (SBS) Transit Limited or SMRT Bus Limited.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the holder leaves the employment of an operator to work for another, the licence is no longer valid and the new employer would have to submit a fresh application.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, we have new and more bus operators coming into the industry by virtue of the Government contracting model.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To alleviate the manpower situation in the industry, can the Ministry consider making ODVL transferable?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would facilitate our bus captains to start work at the new company without waiting for the reapplication of the licence, which can sometimes take up to an average of two months from the first point of application.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we need to enhance the career progression pathway for bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To do so, we need to provide a centralised structured training framework which can help deepen one's professional skills and, consequently, lead to progressive wages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Continuous training programmes should also be made accessible to bus captains at all stages of their career, for them to learn and acquire new skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, in the past, bus captains had to do manual engine checks by lifting the heavy bonnet.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, the checks can be conducted by simply using the dashboard at the driver's seat.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, the training of bus captains is decentralised to the respective public bus operators.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A centralised training centre would be useful so as to standardise the basic training programmes for bus captains as well as to provide continuous training in a structured manner for them to keep up with environmental changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on any plans to enhance the training programmes for our bus captains?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, due to the demanding working conditions of bus captains and the gradual ageing profile, the union is naturally concerned about their health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, timely that we holistically review the overall working conditions of our bus captains to ensure that they are physically and mentally fit to do their job well.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of the areas we can look at include reviewing their work schedule, ergonomics intervention and fatigue management.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Early detection and intervention can certainly help our bus captains identify and address potential health threats before they fall seriously ill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, we need to stop the abuse of bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During my ground visits, I hear bus captains having bad encounters with commuters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are often at the receiving end of verbal abuse by some commuters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our bus captains are striving to serve the commuters well every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They deserve some respect for their hard work and not abuse.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Khaw Boon Wan, would you wish to report on progress?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They lost their lives while working for SMRT on 22 March 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The thoughts and prayers of the entire transport family are with their families.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The tragedy was a massive blow to all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: There will be a Coroner's Inquiry in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Within the legal constraints, I will share what I can.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our priorities are to establish the cause of the incident and prevent a recurrence.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The investigations will ascertain whether the problem was inadequate safety procedures or if there were human lapses in the execution of such procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If the investigations reveal human errors, those responsible will be held to account.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Workplace safety is the responsibility of the operator.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: When an industrial accident happens, MOM will usually issue a stop-work order and only allow work to resume when investigations are completed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA has shared the same instructions with SBS Transit for compliance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I have directed LTA to also work with SMRT to thoroughly review its safety-related procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our common objective is to prevent such an accident from occurring again.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is dynamic, constantly evolving as it shapes our life and in turn, we reshape it to make our life better.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I appreciate the comments of Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Mr Zaqy Mohamad on the future of transport in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I see four major drivers behind our transport's continuing evolution.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: First, emergence of new technology, such as driverless vehicles, with wide implications on many existing jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Second, introduction of new business models, such as the sharing economy and its current manifestation through Uber and Grab, which benefit commuters but are disrupting the incumbents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Third, continuing greying of our population and the need to ensure that our city is silver-friendly while promoting active ageing to add healthy years to our life.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Fourth, greater urgency to protect our environment through reducing our carbon footprint.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These driving forces are already changing our transport sector in significant ways.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We do not yet know how exactly the future will pan out but we can be sure that transport in, say, 2030 will be Page: 7 very different from today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We use "a car-lite Singapore" to describe this future, but we know it is inadequate to characterise it as just about roads and cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Transport 2030 is much more; it is also about active mobility, high quality first-and-last-mile connectivity, smart and on-demand point-to-point transport options, greater pedestrianisation, more opportunities to appreciate on foot our rich city heritage and greenery, and very much more.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Singapore's transformation in the past 50 years has given us a solid foundation to make a quantum leap forward.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Changes will be incremental but, over 15 years, we shall collectively experience a quantum leap.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our SG50 babies will only be in Secondary school by then.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Unlike our generation, learning to drive may well be a thing of the past, let alone owning four wheels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Japanese have already begun to observe their young's loss of interest in cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They even coined a Japanese phrase for this phenomenon: "kuruma banare", meaning "demotorisation".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Indeed, why is there a need to own a car when you can easily summon up a driverless pod with a few strokes on your mobile phone?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Private cars will likely start to go the way of horse carriages, if not in 15 years, definitely in 20 or 25 years' time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, I agree with Mr Sitoh and Mr Zaqy Mohamad that we need to prepare Singapore, Singaporeans and our industries for this brave new world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We need to start making adjustments and mental preparations now.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Over the current term of Government, the Ministry of Transport (MOT) will progressively put forward the legislative and policy pieces to prepare us for this exciting transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We need to discuss what to do and which to do first.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For this first Committee of Supply of mine as Minister for Transport, I wish to cover three areas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: First, how to enhance accessibility for commuters in particular, how to make it hassle-free for commuters to move from their homes to the nearest train station or bus stop?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have taken some initial steps but these are not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity must make a quantum leap to be among the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Currently, many other cities, like Amsterdam and Copenhagen, do a better job than us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We must close the gap and be better, particularly because we live in the tropics with hotter and wetter weather.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo will outline our approach on First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity and, within that framework, she will respond to the recent recommendations of Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim's Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Second, how to enhance point-to-point transport options for commuters?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The sharing economy and, in particular, new business models like Grab and Uber, are benefiting commuters globally.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But they are disrupting existing business models of taxi-operators, with impact on taxi-drivers, Uber, in particular, is causing havoc in many cities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Many countries have taken the wrong turn by banning Uber.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We should not obstruct innovation, especially when it benefits commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We should be mindful of the disruption to incumbents and help incumbents make the correct adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We should seek to achieve win-win for both the disrupters and the incumbents, with commuter welfare as the underpinning principle.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Later, Senior Minister of State Ng Chee Meng will outline our approach to this development.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Third, how to achieve excellence in public transport, especially in rail?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is a crucial piece if we are to become car-lite.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As pointed out by Mr Sitoh and Mr Zaqy Mohamad, our current car- Page: 8 dominant transport model is not sustainable, given our land constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It needs to be replaced by one that has, as its foundation, an excellent public transport system which is reliable, convenient and smart.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Central to this vision is a reliable rail network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This has been one of my top priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I heard Mr Dennis Tan's comments on train faults and breakdowns.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They, too, want our MRT to be the best.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Six months into the job, my sense is that we are making some improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is what we call "mean kilometre before failure" (MKBF), a common reliability measure widely used globally.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, in two years, we have improved from 93,000 kilometres to 133,000 kilometres.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But 133,000 kilometres is still below Hong Kong's 300,000 kilometres.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We want to catch up with Hong Kong and we will.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This was more than Hong Kong's 12 disruptions in a year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Not as good and we are also working hard on this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I monitor this closely and I have some progress to report.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For us in this trade, we know how difficult it is to achieve such a target.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The other MRT lines are working hard to catch up.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The North-South Line (NSL) has crossed the 93-day mark.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This is our oldest line, nearly 30 years of age and, if there is no incident in the next seven days, NSL will cross the 100 days' mark next week.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If they succeed, their success will be especially inspiring for our team, given its age.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Young or old, each time a line crosses a significant milestone, I visit the maintenance staff to thank them personally and to cheer them on; go for the next milestone.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Even when they fail to cross a milestone, like the North East Line (NEL) which experienced a disruption two months ago, on the very day when they were about to cross the 100-day mark, I visited them to tell them that we appreciated their efforts, regardless.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We lick our wounds, reset the clock, we press on, we work even harder.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Today, NEL has crossed the 68-day mark and I look forward to welcoming them to the "100-day Club" next month.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: What is our strategy to improve rail reliability?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: First, the operators are ramping up their engineering and maintenance resources.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are moving towards preventive maintenance – that is, we monitor the conditions of the assets and do the necessary maintenance before any issues arise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This requires the operators to deploy condition monitoring tools on the trains and on the tracks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Some have already been deployed – the linear variable differential transformer to monitor the condition of the third rail, as well as the wheel impact load detector (WILD) to monitor the train wheels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This year, we expect to deploy even more sensors – a catenary eye system (CES) using infrared to monitor the power system for NEL, and a rolling stock condition monitoring system (RSCMS) to collect information regarding the train systems on NSL and East-West Page: 9 Line (EWL).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These are all very costly investments, but they are necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are aggressively renewing the infrastructure of our rail network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Within two years, we would have completely replaced the sleepers and the third rail on NSL and EWL, and also upgraded their signalling system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Third, we are forging a closer team, between LTA the designer and the train operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We address each incident as a collective responsibility – no finger pointing, share openly and solve the problems speedily.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are tightening regulations and stepping up audits on the maintenance processes, augmenting resources where necessary to get the job done.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA has set up technical advisory panels, such as for our power systems, and has overseas operators on the panels to share their expertise and experience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are learning and benefiting from their insights.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are grateful for their generosity in sharing and advising us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Fifth, we are reskilling and upskilling our engineering and maintenance crew.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We need a quantum leap both in the numbers and in the capabilities of our rail industry, both to up our existing maintenance standards and to cope with a rapidly expanding network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In due course, we hope the Academy will also conduct R&D to contribute to the design of new systems which are easier to build, maintain and operate.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Prof Cham Tao Soon has come forward, volunteered his service to spearhead this initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: He and Mr Tan Gee Paw have been a valuable help to us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They know engineering and they are risking their reputation built up over decades of excellent work in the Civil Service.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They are doing national service for the larger good.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I am grateful to them and to many other seasoned engineers who have come forward to volunteer their services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We all want an MRT system which all Singaporeans can be proud of.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Even as we work hard to improve reliability, we are, in parallel, working to expand the rail capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Actually, the right order of things is to stabilise the system first, before expanding it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I hope Members appreciate the severe pressure on the shoulders and the stress on our engineers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I can see it in their faces, though they never voice it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They are an honest, hardworking and resilient lot; they take their responsibilities seriously and stoically.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These are tough guys, but I think some tender loving care from Singaporeans would be very much appreciated.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Before I leave this subject, let me add three more points.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Adding more trains and running them more frequently exert a heavy load on the power system during peak hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: While the additional load is within the original design capacity of the existing system, we are severely reducing the design buffer.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As engineers, we know the importance of a comfortable buffer, to deal with unforeseen events, for instance, a sudden surge in demand on the rail network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I think Mr Sitoh alluded to this yesterday when he said, "Are we biting Page: 10 off more than we can chew?" I think we are, but what to do?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The solution is to upgrade the power system and build new substations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But such an extensive upgrade on a live system will take a few years to complete.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Meanwhile, we are taking a risk that it may cause more disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are deploying condition monitoring tools and techniques to help mitigate such risks, but we know the risks cannot be fully eliminated.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: So, please be forgiving should you experience a disruption during this very critical transition period.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Second, I want to reiterate an earlier observation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are stepping up maintenance, we are doing major replacement works and we are expanding the system capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Normally, these activities should be done sequentially and in that order, but we are not.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: All these are happening on the ground, on a live rail system, with a small window of only three engineering hours a day.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Ideally, we should provide longer continuous engineering hours and this means shorter revenue service hours.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: I hope commuters will allow us to open some of the MRT lines a bit later in the morning, or close them a bit earlier at night.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: An extra hour or two per day will make a lot of difference to our engineering and maintenance staff and help them perform better.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We can run some buses to provide an alternative.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Experts from London Underground and the Taipei Metro shared with us their past experience in re-signalling which was not at all pleasant.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It took them many months to get it right, with many delays and disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For example, London Underground went through two years of public unhappiness!

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This subject is now adding to what is keeping us awake at night.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As Members may know, we will be changing the signalling system of NSL this year, followed by the EWL next year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will do our best to try to achieve a flawless execution and we are keeping our fingers crossed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Besides new lines, we are upgrading existing lines, as described earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These works cover trains, tracks, signalling systems and also MRT stations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: For example, work will start later this year to upgrade 17 MRT stations, including Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's Khatib station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Following the upgrade, Er Dr Lee's residents will have more standing room and more elderly-friendly seats at the platform.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will also look at expanding bicycle parking.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA will also look into her other suggestions as we continue refreshing our older stations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Besides trains, our rail network must be complemented by a good and reliable bus network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have made significant progress in recent years to increase capacity, improve reliability and enhance service levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We have introduced new bus services and all bus services will run at shorter intervals.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Transition to the bus contracting model is also progressing smoothly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA will be calling the third tender package very soon.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But as noted by Mr Melvin Yong, we also need a few thousand more bus captains to join the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo chairs the Public Transport Tripartite Committee (PTTC), which seeks to professionalise the bus industry, so as to attract more Singaporeans into the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: The Page: 11 Committee will share details of their efforts in the next few months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon asked about the use of electric buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is a promising idea, though the current economics still do not make it viable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But I share his optimism that technological progress and especially in bus battery, will make electric buses viable in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Another promising idea is self-driving vehicles, as noted by Mr Png Eng Huat.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: But it is just a matter of time before such vehicles can be deployed on public roads, whether for private or public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: As I outlined earlier, a fleet of self-driving vehicles plying the neighbourhood will greatly enhance our first-and-last mile connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We are doing several trials and want Singapore to be among the leaders in such concepts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: It is making a "big bet on Singapore", according to its COO.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: They hope to see Singapore among the world's first to commercially deploy self-driving vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: If they or their rivals succeed, it will impact existing taxi drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: This means that we must put the MRT to optimal use and the bus services must dovetail and complement the MRT.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We must also keep improving the bus and taxi services and keep the growth of cars to moderate levels." This principle has guided our transport strategy ever since.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: At SG51, it is even clearer that a car-dominant model cannot underpin Singapore's next phase of development.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We need to facilitate new transport technology, change mind-sets and go car-lite.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: Our public transport must make a quantum leap.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We will, therefore, be relentless in pursuing rail excellence, improving our bus service and instituting a future-friendly regulatory and policy framework.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We must allow various forms of point-to-point mobility to flourish in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: At the same time, we must rethink and adjust existing car and car parking policies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: London, Paris and many Japanese cities have introduced car-free days and reduced car parking norms.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: These are measures to help reset their motorists' attitude towards cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: In addition, we want Singaporeans to come to cherish public transport as an indispensable part of their daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: LTA will continue to forge among Singaporeans this sense of ownership and pride in our public buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: And I will make sure that this pride extends to our MRT, too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Khaw Boon Wan)
text: We need some more time but we will get there, during this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Currently, despite the high costs of driving to work, many people still grit their teeth, bear the ERP charges and bear the expensive parking charges because they have limited options of getting to office and back home.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: One option is to provide better connectivity from the private estates to the nearest MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Within my constituency, I have many residents living in the condominiums at Meyer, Amber, Haig Road and Tanjong Rhu.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If they have a better option of a bus service to the nearest MRT station, I am confident that many of these drivers will leave their cars behind and take public transport to work.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: During my dialogues with residents, many of them have requested for a shuttle bus service to bring them to the nearest MRT station during the morning and evening peak hours.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Their feedback is that the train station is not that far off, about 1.5 to two kilometres away, but the weather in Singapore is too hot and too humid for them to walk too long a distance to the nearest MRT station.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Imagine if we are able to persuade 20% to 30% of these drivers to leave their cars behind and take public transport to work because it is just as convenient and less expensive than their cars.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If the bus journey is a round-trip service, this would take a bus only about 15 to 20 minutes to make one round trip and pick up the next batch of commuters.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This will strongly encourage commuters who used to drive, to leave their cars at home and use public transport as a choice mode of travel.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: So, Minister, this will alleviate road congestion during peak hours and will be environmentally friendlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Any cyclist can pick up a bicycle near their home, ride to the nearest MRT station and park the bicycle there.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In the evening, they can pick up any bicycle and ride home and park at the bicycle station near their homes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This will be akin to the bicycle rental scheme available in cities like London, Paris and Taipei.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If these cities can do so, I believe Singapore can do so, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Elderly residents are more vulnerable when travelling along public roads.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If there is proper coordination and implementation of the green wave for vehicles, traffic speeds will not be adversely affected as all traffic lights along the same stretch of road would be green or red at the same time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I had, over the past few years, appealed to MOT for a lift to be built at the pedestrian overhead bridge at the Tanjong Rhu area to allow the elderly residents to cross the road safely.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Because Page: 13 Tanjong Rhu is an old estate, it has a high proportion of elderly residents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It does pain me to see the elderly struggling to climb the high pedestrian overhead bridge as they head towards the market.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: If the signalised crossing is aligned to the traffic lights at the next main road junction, it will not impede traffic flow since the green wave conditions will allow traffic to flow smoothly at the same time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The interest of the elderly residents should always be paramount when reviewing policies and I know that the Minister for Transport thinks in the same manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With an ageing population, there will be more pressure on these lifts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A single lift also means a single point of failure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The priority queue system by itself cannot address all these points.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOT look into building at least two lifts for all stations as a long-term goal?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a burden to wheelchair users with modest means who need to travel regularly to locations less accessible by public transport.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While transport allowance schemes are in place and some VWOs have programmes in place to address this, these are not always available to those in need.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could MOT work with taxi companies to find ways to address the needs of this group, a group which will grow as the population ages?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, can we do more to ensure safety for wheelchair users on our public buses?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current practice on buses is just to place the wheelchair rear-facing, back against the vertical wall and apply the brakes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: WTORS defines different securement systems including the four-point tie-down system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vehicles provided by some VWOs to ferry wheelchair users already use the four-point tie-down system today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I propose that our public buses be required to conform to international standards to ensure safety.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the new buses on display have a seat belt system to improve safety but this is still below international safety standards like WTORS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, my residents and myself have identified some gaps between the shelters which make the walk less Page: 14 pleasant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister can help to plug the gaps.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While I am glad that the Minister, in response to my Parliamentary Question last month, agreed to build a covered walkway from Little India MRT station to KK Women's and Children's Hospital, what about Changi General Hospital?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Are there plans to connect these hospitals to MRT stations with sheltered walkways?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope MOT has a comprehensive plan to build covered walkways for existing public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I know that new hospitals are all linked to the nearest MRT station by covered walkways.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Elderly patients or those who are ill and need to make frequent visits to the hospitals without cars, as well as hospital staff, will greatly appreciate being able to travel to hospitals in comfort instead of having to brave the rain or broiling sun.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: HDB does not want to do it because the pedestrian paths are under the jurisdiction of LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: LTA is also unwilling to because it is only mandated to build sheltered walkways that connect amenities and schools to bus stops and MRT stations and not HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, from the school to the nearest HDB block at Block 310, Jurong East Street 32, is unsheltered, despite repeated requests from my residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, if it rains, children from the schools taking public buses will be dry while children walking home via Block 310 will get wet.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am sure many constituencies also face similar problems.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that LTA can take a holistic view when building sheltered walkways, to think about the needs of the residents in totality and not in terms of which zones they are overseeing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, I hope that LTA can encourage building owners to build their own covered walkways to link with those built by LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Again, these are also neglected zones which do not fall under anybody's jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One example which constitutes a poor last-mile connection is the Civil Service Club at Bukit Batok.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I want to state upfront this Civil Service Club at Bukit Batok is not under the jurisdiction of Bukit Batok.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is under the jurisdiction of Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am not raising this issue because of the impending Bukit Gombak by-election, I must declare that.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: LTA has kindly built a sheltered walkway 150 metres away from the nearest bus stop to the side gate of this Club.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But from the side gate, there is a short gap of about 10 to 20 metres, not covered, before it reaches the sheltered staircase leading to the main building.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For some reason, the Civil Service Club is not covering this path with a shelter.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the event of a heavy downpour, a pedestrian can stay nice and dry for 150 metres and will get drenched before he reaches the Club.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We have marginally missed the last-mile connection and wasted the benefits of the 150-metre shelter.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Once again, I hope LTA will work with the respective building owners to enhance the last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I applaud the Ministry's focus on the long-term needs of Singapore even as it beefs up our current capacity.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Compared to other leading cities in the world, however, we do not seem to have as comprehensive a last-mile connectivity as other cities do.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: So, in the spirit of contributing to a world-class transport system, let me mention a few examples.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In Canada, they have built an underground city named RESO right in downtown Montreal.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: RESO consists of 32 kilometres of tunnels spreading over a 12-square kilometres area.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: By comparison, our Orchard Road shopping belt is only 2.2 	kilometres long.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The underground city includes 60 residential and commercial complexes linking hotels, shopping malls, banks, corporate headquarters, museums, university buildings, seven metro stations, two commuter train stations and the Bell Centre hockey arena.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This is equivalent to an indoor stadium of 21,000 seats.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: There are more than 120 exterior access points to this underground city.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Nearly 500,000 people use the underground city per day, especially to escape Montreal's harsh winters.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In another Canadian city, Toronto, there is an elaborate Downtown Underground Pedestrian Walkway called PATH.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It claims to be the world's largest, continuous underground shopping complex with 30 	kilometres of shopping arcades.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: PATH has approximately 1,200 shops and services, employing 5,000 people.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Commuters can access more than 50 buildings and office towers, 20 parking garages, six subway stations, two major departmental stores, eight major hotels and a railway terminal.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Commuters can also get to some of Toronto's major tourist attractions, such as the Hockey Hall, Roy Thomson Hall, the Air Canada Centre, Rogers Centre and the CN Tower.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Closer home, Japanese cities show how underground space development can be maximised.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: According to Japan Times, Tokyo has approximately 63,000 underground areas, 40% of which are underground paths, subway systems and shopping complexes.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The eight largest underground shopping areas in the capital add up to about 214,000 square meters – about the same as having five Tokyo Stadiums buried underground.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: One could walk from the Otemachi station to Higashi-ginza station, all via underground over a 4.05-kilometre walkway.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This is about the walking distance between our Newton station and City Hall station in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For those of us who have travelled to Hong Kong and Taipei, we also see similar underground walkway infrastructure which render the cities walkable.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In Singapore, most of our efforts to improve last-mile connectivity have been focused on sheltered linkways.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: More recently, MOT has reaffirmed its vision to enhance our last-mile connectivity to promote "walking, cycling, and riding public transport" as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Beyond sheltered linkways, we have heard little about our plans to build more underground spaces and walkways, especially in the City Core areas.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Building owners often cite cost and technical challenges as key deterrents.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Some also believe that the laws governing subterranean development can be further enhanced to catalyse new investments.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Would the Ministry, in consideration of the larger and long-term good for Singapore and as the lead agency responsible for last-mile connectivity, champion Singapore's underground space developments, especially in the City Core area?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on how the newly-amended State Land Act and Land Acquisition Act would facilitate such a lead role MOT might play?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Walking more on a daily basis could help many average Singaporeans to reduce the risk of obesity, diabetes and other heart-related diseases.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While this recommendation will certainly help to reduce the risks that cyclists face on the road, the risk for pedestrians also increases.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In reality, a number of cyclists are already riding on footpaths and there are many accounts of cyclists and users of PMDs who do not give way to pedestrians nor stop when approaching bus stops or crowded areas like neighbourhood centres and markets.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While residents understand the need to legalise PMDs on footpaths, I hope that we can continue to educate our cyclists on good practices, such as dismounting in crowded places.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It would take additional planning and investments to do this but I do think it will be money well-spent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although it is not presently allowed, we often see bicycles on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If introduced, steps should be taken to ensure that cyclists use the footpaths in accordance with any new rules and also with good practices, such as giving way and keeping left.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 17 I agree with the recommendations for speed limits, use of helmet and use of standard bicycle lights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Bicycle lights are important safety devices, especially in the evenings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is often difficult for motorists to spot a cyclist riding at night without any lights until one is almost caught up with the cyclist.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether it is bicycle lights, use of helmet or cycling on footpaths and any new measures which the Ministry should choose to adopt, I feel that if there is no effective public education and effective enforcement, especially early on after the introduction of the new measures, such measures will never be adopted by many cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to suggest that for reasons of safety, there should be a rule for keeping left, whether on footpaths, connectors or on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An example of PMA is the motorised device used by the elderly or people with some form of mobility constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for the suggested ban on the use of PMAs on roads to work effectively and reasonably, there must be user-friendly pavements along every road; otherwise, such a ban will not be practical or fair.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PMDs include electric skate scooters and kick scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such scooters are regularly seen on the roads now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, public education, coupled with effective enforcement, will be important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, with these safety measures, it may be suitable to let e-bikes to be used on park connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can often see people with illegally modified e-bikes on the roads or connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Presently, the onus is on the manufacturers to apply to LTA for their e-bikes to be authorised by LTA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, unauthorised e-bikes are still available for sale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many e-bikes which are in use are not authorised models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be harsh to expect them to stop the use of their bikes when they can comply with the new rules.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the issue of registration of e-bikes, I think this is a good method of ensuring bike owners use their e-bikes responsibly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Panel has also recommended against allowing e-bikes which are powered by throttle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have received feedback that throttle may be more suitable for some users, such as the elderly, as they do not need some strength to paddle and kick in the electric power required in current authorised models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Control of speed by throttle is also more precise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As long as the maximum speed of the bike is limited, the throttle does not make the bike unsafe.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, PMAs, or even PMDs like e-scooters, are powered by technology which is similar to throttle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, unlike e-bikes, safety may not be an issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, whatever measures adopted may only work if there is sufficient public education and effective enforcement, especially at the onset.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must be sufficient resources and the willingness for all authorities responsible for enforcing the use of bicycles on roads, cycling paths, footpaths and connectors to make the proposed new cycling rules work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last but not least, may I compliment the good efforts and determination of members of the Panel led by Parliamentary Secretary Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ball is now in the Ministry's court.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have heard of many cases of residents who had bad experiences with errant cyclists.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, I support cycling as a healthy activity and an environmentally responsible way of getting around.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, it is difficult to enforce responsible cycling behaviour and it is almost impossible to get errant cyclists to take on responsibility for their victims, unlike in traffic accidents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They do not even take the Highway Code.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no recourse for the victim and also no proper legal framework for insurance claims or resolution of disputes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a few weeks ago, I stood near the junction of Bedok Reservoir Road and Jalan Eunos to assess the flow and egress of residents' vehicles from Bedok Reservoir Road and their complaints of cyclists who dashed across the zebra crossing to catch the flashing "Green Man" across the Jalan Eunos pedestrian crossing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the hour or so I was at the junction, not a single cyclist, either a foreign worker, Singaporean or PR, stopped to dismount from their bicycle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Rather, there were quite a few glares from drivers towards cyclists and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In practice, the Ministry could consider how the stop line works for drivers in the US.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Regardless whether there is traffic or not, every driver stops at the stop line or risks a fine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of our crowded shared spaces during peak hours, such a clear rule is likely to make our footpaths, bus stops and pedestrian crossings safer, especially for our elderly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In particular, who will be enforcing the rules and code of conduct governing the use of PMDs and bicycles on footpaths and cycling paths?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Will MOT engage traffic wardens or even residents to enforce the rules and the codes of conduct?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What will be the penalty if cyclists or persons using PMDs do not follow the rules?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Next, I would like to turn my attention to e-bikes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It is important that retailers only sell LTA's approved e-bikes and facilitate the registration of e-bikes as they are sold.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I trust that LTA will set up a system to make registration of e-bikes a seamless process.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: LTA may also want to consider mandating the e-bike user to pass an abridged Highway Code for the safety of e-bike users, pedestrians and other road users.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How would LTA mandate existing e-bike users to register?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Would they be given a timeframe to register?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What are the enforcement measures to deter e-bike users from using the pedestrian pathways or bicycle paths?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: While the recommendations of AMAP are good, there remain many unanswered questions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I hope that the Senior Minister of State for Transport Mrs Josephine Teo will share with us the details of its implementation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: AMAP has issued a list of recommendations on the rules and code of conduct expected of cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree that it is more important that they behave in a safe and considerate manner rather than focus on having more enforcement.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was recommended that e-bikes should be allowed on cycling paths and shared paths, but at a speed limit.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Panel also recommends that the Government consider registering e-bikes to facilitate identification and enforcement against errant riders.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, illegally modified e-bikes may have more powerful motors and some even have throttles installed.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some may even go up to the same speed as motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, they are a potential danger on the roads and shared paths.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Repeat offenders may be charged in Court and have their e-bikes seized.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, retailers found to continue selling non-compliant e-bikes or workshop operators modifying them illegally will be charged in Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also hear of incidents involving e-bikes and other vehicles on the roads, or with pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides educating e-bike users to exercise caution, there should also be stricter enforcement on illegal modifications and sale of unapproved models.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that when LTA engages retailers and workshops to update them on the changes in the technical requirements and penalties for not conforming, they should also consider involving them Page: 20 in educating buyers on safe riding.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, in their education and enforcement efforts, LTA should also cover e-bike rental operators or delivery companies who issue employees the use of company owned e-bikes, even though these may not be as prevalent at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that we also anticipate and address situations where dormitory owners may rent out e-bikes for their residents or other commercial users —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang, please conclude your speech, your time is up.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Furthermore, will we also consider banning e-bikes on the expressway?

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will expand on a key theme in MOT's COS debate this year – that of enhancing accessibility for commuters, in particular, our plans to make it hassle-free for commuters to move from their homes to the nearest train station or bus stop.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Minister Khaw described earlier, we crystallise these efforts as First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity (FLMC).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will bring our MRT network much closer to where Singaporeans work and live.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In around five years, no matter where you are in the city area, a train station will only be five minutes away.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The expanded rail network will be much more beneficial if we also improve their accessibility to commuters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We share the same belief, as members like Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Mr Ang Wei Neng, that there has been progress on FLMC and more is achievable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our goal is for Singapore to make a quantum leap, to be among the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To get to where we envision Singapore, we must close the gap with cities like Amsterdam and Copenhagen and aim to do better, particularly because we live in the tropics with hotter, wetter, more humid weather.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will outline our approach on FLMC and, within that framework, respond to the recent recommendations of Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal's AMAP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the next few years, every resident will be able to reap the benefits of the upcoming FLMC improvements in their neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want everyone, including the less mobile like our seniors and persons with disabilities, to be able to get to their nearby MRT station or bus interchange comfortably, conveniently and safely, whether it is by walking, cycling or using PMD.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: FLMC considerations are fully integrated into the design and construction of new stations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example: (a) DTL 2 stations will be served by 13 kilometres of sheltered walkways; and (b) DTL 3 stations will go slightly further; they will be served by 16 kilometres of sheltered walkways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Page: 21 There are 56 kilometres of sheltered walkways today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, if you add those 56 kilometres to what DTLs 2 and 3 will have – we are talking about 85 kilometres – that is one end of Singapore to the other and back.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Existing stations will be fitted out under LTA's Walk2Ride programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So far, we already have sheltered walkways for about 40% of all MRT stations across Singapore and more will follow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond the immediate vicinity of train stations, LTA will work with other stakeholders to make our towns more walkable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
