text: For example, HDB and Town Councils co-share the responsibility of improving the walking experience within towns with LTA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will follow up on suggestions like those of Mr Ang Wei Neng, for more covered walkways to link HDB blocks to nearby amenities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Ang also suggested that LTA build covered walkways from MRT stations to nearby hospitals, in particular, Changi General Hospital and Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Members know, under our Walk2Ride framework, LTA gives priority to connecting hospitals within 400 metres of MRT stations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because this is a distance most commuters are willing to cover on foot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, Khoo Teck Puat Hospital is about 700 metres away from Yishun MRT station, and a little bit more, if we consider the actual walking route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At such a distance, commuters tend to prefer a bus transfer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, we will study the feasibility of a sheltered walkway later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Meanwhile, the free shuttle buses, as well as public feeder buses, will continue to serve commuters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There will be more direct routes and options for walking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Both Mr Ang and Mr Sitoh have noted that some walkways can be circuitous and add many minutes to the walk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I agree with them fully that more direct routes will make walking a more attractive option for commuters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Now, sometimes, large plots of privately-owned land and buildings can get in the way of a more direct walking route.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But thanks to the support of our colleagues in MND and URA, private developers will be required to submit a Walking and Cycling Plan when they apply for URA's planning approval.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Essentially, this plan will require developers to propose how they would design their buildings to provide safe and convenient access and infrastructure for pedestrians, as well as cyclists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA and URA will share more details shortly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Ang also asked whether we could encourage building owners to build or link up their covered walkways to those built by the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA already does so, although it remains the building owners' prerogative to decide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similarly, we are trying to connect our expanding transport network to more buildings via underground links, as suggested by Mr Lee Yi Shyan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I must thank Mr Lee for sharing many interesting examples with us and also for reminding Members of the health benefits of walking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, our plans include elevated off-road pedestrian walkways, such as those linking the twin towers of Ng Teng Fong Hospital to the nearby Jurong East station and adjacent shopping malls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I recently took a short but enjoyable walk there.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I think it is called "J-Walk" but it is entirely legal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The linkways make very good sense, given our local weather, and we should have more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong has recently explained the approach which MND and MOT will jointly implement, which most likely involves further legislative change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Page: 22 URA is the lead agency working with LTA and there is already an underground masterplan which includes the central area underground pedestrian network.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are an important group of commuters that we must take care of, either because they are less mobile by age or disability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Leon Perera spoke about their needs, as did Ms Chia Yong Yong during the Budget debate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As part of the Government's Action Plan for Successful Ageing, LTA is putting in more seats at new MRT stations for seniors to rest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And, indeed, we are considering equipping new stations with two sets of lifts each – that is something that Mr Leon Perera asked about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA will also build signalised pedestrian crossings, rather than overhead bridges or underpasses, where possible, as the elderly and persons with disabilities do find it physically less taxing to use signalised pedestrian crossings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA is looking at different standards for wheelchair users, including Wheelchair Tie-down and Occupant Restraint Systems (WTORS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where there are overhead bridges, the Government has a programme to install lifts at frequently-used ones, so that the less mobile can still cross the roads with minimal difficulty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am sympathetic to Mr Lim Biow Chuan's appeals for a lift to be built at a specific overhead bridge and I commend his diligence as the Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Lim knows, the overhead bridge is already fitted with a ramp.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given our need to provide barrier-free access to as many bridges as possible, we have to focus on bridges that do not yet have any form of barrier-free access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I seek his understanding as there are residents in every estate who are waiting for such lifts to be installed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will study the possibility of a signalised pedestrian crossing; the primary consideration being the safety of pedestrians, especially seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides walking, many train commuters use feeder buses to get to the MRT stations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, FLMCs via some 64 feeder bus services are generally good.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most residents, including those living in private estates, have a bus stop within a five-minute walk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To encourage more people from private estates to take public transport, Mr Lim Biow Chuan suggested providing peak hour shuttle bus services to connect MRT stations and private estates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are open to providing public buses, especially if it is assessed that ridership will reach a certain minimum level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There should be reasonable cost recovery; otherwise, the service will not be well used and the resources should be redeployed to areas where more residents can be served.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a fair approach to assessing the regular requests for bus services and LTA can work with Mr Lim and other advisers to make the necessary assessments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So far, Madam, I have spoken on what we are doing for pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is an important priority for us because almost every public transport user would need to walk at some point in their journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But more and more Singaporeans are making their connections to the public transport Page: 23 network or getting around their neighbourhood in another way – by cycling and using PMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a small, but rapidly expanding group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Their profile is quite diverse, ranging from neighbourhood "uncles" and "aunties", to students going to school and parents sending their kids to and from childcare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As many Members would be aware, we are building dedicated intra-town cycling networks for every HDB town as quickly as we can.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, Ang Mo Kio will be a demonstration project as we test out additional infrastructure, such as seamless cycling and walking corridors below the MRT viaduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If these experiments work well, we can replicate them in other towns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also suggested providing bike-sharing services to connect MRT stations and private estates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are, indeed, keen to test out how bike-sharing can help improve first-and-last-mile connections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will pilot bike-sharing services in the Jurong Lake District next year, learn from this pilot and see how we can bring it to other residential areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Miss Cheng Li Hui noted, dedicated cycling paths are really the most ideal and safest option for cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, I fully share their concerns for pedestrians, especially seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But the reality is that we have limited land and much of Singapore which the public regularly accesses is already quite built-up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is, therefore, not realistic to build dedicated cycling paths everywhere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For cycling and use of PMDs to become viable first-and-last-mile options soon, rather than far into the future, we need an environment and culture where pedestrians and cyclists, as well as users of PMDs, are willing and able to share space.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To consult the public on how we can foster such an environment and culture, we set up AMAP in July last year, and the members were drawn from a broad spectrum of society and were led by Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, my former MOT colleague, who remains very passionate about active mobility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Panel submitted its report to the Government last month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I commend and thank the Panel for their detailed work and well-considered recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They have taken in as many views as possible and made some very difficult trade-offs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Overall, the recommendations are fair and balanced, with sensible rules and guidelines to ensure the safety of pedestrians, cyclists and users of PMDs alike.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Page: 24 These new rules significantly improve the mobility options for everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our seniors and persons with disabilities will find it easier to get around their neighbourhoods using motorised wheelchairs or mobility scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Students will find it safer to cycle to school; parents have more peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Families cycling to town centres for their daily activities or to catch a train will also be safer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the other hand, we fully recognise the safety concerns of pedestrians in sharing the footpaths with faster moving users, as pointed out by Mr Gan, Miss Cheng and Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is why the Panel had also proposed a set of rules and code of conduct and policies on speed limits and maximum weight and size of permissible devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Education and enforcement will also be important, as many Members have pointed out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, on education – how do we foster a culture of safety and consideration for others?

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through a mix of outdoor, online and printed media, we will explain the new policies and rules and their rationale.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also encourage cyclists and users of PMDs to pledge their commitment to riding safely on footpaths, shared paths and cycling paths through various activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be supplemented by more in-depth education on safe cycling through a new Cyclist Education Programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Participants will be taught how to be safe and considerate around others, how to use cycling infrastructure properly and practise what they have learnt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, a shift in culture is a shared responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To change habits and evolve new ones, to contribute to a culture where all users of shared paths conduct themselves with consideration for others, we need the involvement and ownership of the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I agree with Mr Ang that it is important to cast the net wide when engaging these partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA will partner community interest groups, grassroots organisations, retailers of bicycles and PMDs and others to help spread key education messages in their respective communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, we will work with the grassroots to set up volunteer Active Mobility Patrols.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is modelled after the cycling warden programme that has been successfully implemented in Tampines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some of you from Tampines GRC may already know Mr Steven Yeo.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He is a long-time volunteer cycling warden and he believes strongly in the role of education to change behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has taken 10 years to develop this sharing culture in Tampines, but he feels that the end result is fulfilling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cyclists in Tampines have become more considerate and the most encouraging indicator is that they maintain safe cycling habits even when the wardens are not around.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Moving on to enforcement and how we step up deterrence, cyclists and PMD users should always care for and give way to pedestrians, who are gracious in sharing the space with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just like how cyclists do not wish to be endangered by motorists on the road, they should spare a thought for pedestrians and avoid being a menace on footpaths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government will step up enforcement against reckless cyclists and users of PMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: NParks will also play their part by conducting targeted enforcement in parks and park connectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also increase penalties for stronger deterrence against reckless behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Page: 25 Miss Cheng asked how we will be enforcing the speed limits on footpaths and cycling paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is not practical to station enforcement officers at every corner – I think we all know that – nor should we be overly rigid by penalising users for going slightly above the speed limit by one kilometre per hour or two kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For a start, we will focus on hotspots, such as crowded bus stops, and use speed guns to help us identify those who are speeding excessively and posing a danger to pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the same vein, AMAP was particularly concerned about the proliferation of illegally modified power-assisted bicycles, or e-bikes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Panel recommended registering these devices for more effective enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We hope to be able to share more information by the end of this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee called for stricter enforcement against retailers of non-compliant e-bikes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Dennis Tan also provided several suggestions, for example, allowing throttles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the meantime, we will need to study the details carefully, make the necessary legislative changes and ramp up our resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even after these changes are implemented on paper, it will not all be smooth sailing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will take time for everyone to get used to the new policies and rules and to cultivate the habits and culture of safe sharing of paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some conflicts will inevitably occur, but I believe that, with time and strong education and enforcement efforts, we will be able to develop a culture of safe and gracious sharing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the right direction to go and we are taking an important first step, but the journey will be a long one spanning many years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will have to make adjustments along the way, by continuing to take in feedback and constantly engaging the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Once again, I would like to thank Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim and his Panel for their very good work in putting forward a set of recommendations to MOT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim has also graciously agreed to MOT's requests to continue to chair the Panel, which will advise on the implementation process and champion this worthy development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where would we like to see ourselves in 15 years?

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Tokyo, a familiar city for many Singaporeans, offers a good preview.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are only about 10 kilometres of dedicated cycling paths in Tokyo, yet pedestrians, cyclists and motorists coexist harmoniously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan also reminded us about their extensive underground pedestrian network.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For all of these, the most important ingredient in Tokyo's success is the people's civic-mindedness and consideration for others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such changes in habits and culture will take time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we are making a good start and with perseverance, we have a good chance of becoming an attractive walking and cycling city, where the first and last mile are among the best that any city can offer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If not, I would urge them to do so and to design the charging model to ensure that total revenue collection remains more or less neutral relative to the current distances travelled and current vehicle population.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The purpose of the ERP system should be to ease congestion and not to raise revenue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I suggest that the aggregated and anonymised data be made accessible in real time and in a user-friendly manner to the private sector so that third-party app developers can provide innovative solutions to motorists, making Singapore a testbed for such innovations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Thirdly, the Government has provided assurances that data privacy will be upheld.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The US Department of Homeland Security, for example, conducts PIAs for several of its programmes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would also like to ask if Government agencies will have limitless access to these data or will there be safeguards against executive over-reach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For example, if the Police want access to information on someone's travel patterns, will they need a Court Order or can they do so without one?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The motor vehicle industry players have been appealing to the Government to smoothen the supply of COEs and to avoid cyclical retrenchment and mass recruitment of staff.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At the same time, wild-swinging COE prices have encouraged premature de-registrations of relatively new vehicles in the past, which is a wastage and not pro-environment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Hence, we would like to know if MOT has plans to further regulate the supply of COEs in the coming year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Page: 27 The growing proportion of Category B or Cat B COE, vis-à-vis that of other categories, is also a concern.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, 10% in year 2000, 28% this year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This is because Open Category or Cat E COE received at least 10% of the de-registrations in each category and Cat E COEs are mainly used to register the CAT B vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Such a phenomenon has unfairly disadvantaged Singaporeans who just want to buy a basic car out of necessity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thus, I would like to urge MOT to consider a reset of the COE distribution to make the system more equitable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it would take a generation to wean cars from our culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For some, owning a car would remain an aspiration or a status symbol.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many others, owning a car is felt as a necessity, especially young families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a car-lite Singapore, cars will become even more a scarcity than it is today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, the socioeconomic inequality and wealth gap between Singaporeans will become reflected in car ownership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government created Category A or Cat A for social equity reasons and had to recategorise it recently to keep the Category for mass-market car buyers after luxury car buyers swamped the category and drove up prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like the Additional Buyer Stamp Duty for the property market, a carefully calibrated COE surcharge would help to reduce overconsumption on the part of the wealthy and help achieve some equity in the car market, especially in favour of young middle-income families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand a version of such a proposal was considered and rejected in 2013 by LTA after public consultation due to the belief that it would be difficult to implement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this is to be the reason again, would the Ministry explain the difficulties in implementation?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another colleague of mine had also touched on this issue during last year's COS debate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans utilised their lower capacity motorcycles for work and to feed their families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As such, an abolition or review of the COE will be a much-needed boost for them, especially in the weakening economy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The then Minister of Transport Mr Lui Tuck Yew, in a response to my question on whether LTA will consider splitting the COE for motorcycles into three categories Page: 28 according to the engine capacity of the motorcycles, which correspond to the class 2, 2A and 2B licences, said that, "splitting would result in a much smaller quota in each sub-category and this may lead to more volatility in quota and prices." I would like to propose that the available Cat D quota for class 2B, class 2A and class 2 motorcycles be allocated in accordance with the percentage of these vehicles on our road.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This means to say that if the average class 2B motorcycle population on our road is 75%, then 75% of the available Cats D to E quotas will be allocated to class 2B motorcycles, adjusted according to the demand.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe this move will address many of the concerns, as expressed in the Minister's reply to my Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: An estimated 40.1% of the total renewal in 2015 chose a 10-year renewal term, compared to an estimated average of 63.4% between 2010 and 2014.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Due to higher COE prices, more motorcycle owners are compelled to renew their COE every five years instead of 10.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Transportation is very challenging and we appreciate MOT's hard work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many motorcyclists in my constituency shared with me that in times of peak congestion, for example, at traffic light junctions, motorcyclists in Singapore ride in between cars.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If so, this means that motorcycles could lead to a smaller impact on peak congestions than many of us previously assumed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Since we are re-evaluating our overall traffic pricing model with the upcoming satellite ERP system, can we consider increasing COEs for motorcycles by perhaps 5% to 15%?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This could decrease the motorcycle COE prices considerably, without increasing the impact on congestions significantly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to hearing MOT's view on this matter.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The high cost of COEs for commercial vehicles not only affects companies but even sole proprietors, such as hawkers and wet market stall-holders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One stall-holder selling fish at the wet market told me that he is going to retire once the COE for his van expires because a new van would Page: 29 cost $80,000 to $100,000 and he will not be able to recoup the cost selling a few "ikan kuning" for $3.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we do not adjust the current formula, we may even end up with a situation where there may be no Cat C COEs available for bidding when there is a high number of vehicles registered under the Early Turnover Scheme.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we justify a deviation from the formula?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, quotas for Cat E draws from Cat A to Cat D equally.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, each of Cat A to Cat D contributes 10% of their quota to Cat E.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This percentage has been reduced recently but was as high as 25% in 2012.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, over the years, while Cat C for commercial vehicles has contributed quota to Cat E, most of the COEs under the Cat E were used for bigger passenger cars.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While drivers of bigger passenger cars have alternatives, such as taking public transport or switching to a smaller car, there are no alternatives available for commercial vehicle users.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, because of the factors mentioned above, even though our economy has grown substantially since 2008, the number of commercial vehicles on our roads has remained constant at around 150,000 over the past seven years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As our economy grows, it is logical that the number of commercial vehicles must grow in tandem to support our businesses.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Meanwhile, we should consider adjusting the formula such that a higher percentage for the Early Turnover Scheme is deducted from Cat E.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Minister Khaw noted, the emergence of new technology is transforming our transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nowhere is this more evident than in the area of point-to-point transport services, especially in the area where taxis are providing this service today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Since I joined MOT some six months ago, I have had the pleasure of getting to know some of our 55,000 active taxi drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our taxi drivers take great pride in their profession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Good taxi drivers know their routes and where and when customers are likely to be waiting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They plan their routes well, try very hard to avoid traffic jams and provide good customer service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singaporeans recognise that, generally, our taxi industry has served their needs adequately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This, of course, is, in large part, due to Page: 30 our taxi drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, more are taking bookings via apps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is partly because our taxi companies have improved their own booking apps, with smarter algorithms to match commuters' needs with the drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have done this more efficiently and better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Third-party taxi apps, on the other hand, have helped to aggregate supply and demand at the industry level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As a result, both taxi commuters and drivers have benefited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Taxi drivers, especially those from the smaller taxi companies, tell me that they get more jobs from bookings and earn more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Indeed, taxi drivers' incomes have increased continuously over the past three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, not all the levers for responding to the new environment are in the taxi companies' and drivers' hands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One common feedback I receive from taxi drivers is that the training curriculum for the Taxi Driver Vocational Licence (TDVL) should be updated to reflect technological developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, we should no longer focus as much on memorising the street directory for route planning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should instead also teach our drivers to use GPS and online navigational tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I hope this incentive can lead to better services which would, ultimately, benefit commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Technology has also transformed chauffeured services to become an attractive alternative to taxi services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The entry of Uber and GrabCar has made chauffeured services more accessible to the general public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mobile apps can now match individual passengers with a chauffeured car service quickly and on a per-trip basis, rather than on a per-hour basis or perday basis, as it was previously in the chauffeured industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 drivers provide chauffeured services during peak hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This has effectively increased the supply of point-to-point transport services by about a third during these hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many commuters I have met have told me that they really appreciate how chauffeured services supplement taxi services, especially during periods when taxis are in short supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Most of the drivers providing chauffeured services are part-timers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One such driver, Mrs Rennu Mahajan, a mother to two sons and also a real estate agent, shared that she has been a part-time GrabCar driver since August 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She explained to me that she enjoys the flexible hours where she can have her time with family while also earning some extra income in a rather quiet real estate market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The growth of chauffeured services has benefited commuters, but the new competition has understandably caused some disquiet among some taxi drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While Mr Ang Hin Kee did not quite raise the issues in Parliament today, in our course of discussion when he was representing NTA, we had discussed many pertinent points about the disrupting effect on the taxi drivers, so I will take the time now to address some of these points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 31 The responses from some cities like Paris, Brussels and Rio de Janeiro have taken what I think is the wrong approach, by creating protectionist regulations or banning chauffeured services entirely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Such an approach ultimately leads to a poorer outcome for commuters and risks fossilising the taxi industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Fortunately for us, we are in a much better position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our taxi industry has generally been well-run, based on sound market principles and not excessively regulated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We do not rely on a medallion system or an expensive taxi permit licensing system to limit the entry of new taxis or drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Therefore, our taxi drivers are not in heavy debt, unlike some in Paris or Florence where a taxi driver must pay anywhere from €200,000 to €300,000 euros just for the privilege or the right to provide taxi services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have opened up our industry and deregulated fares for many years now and so the industry in Singapore has remained competitive and market-responsive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With our good foundation, we are better able to move with the times and reap the benefits of technology improvements and innovations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Like for the Taxi Driver Vocational Licence, this framework ensures that drivers providing chauffeured services undergo sufficient training on safety and the regulations for providing such services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Applicants will also undergo background screening and be subjected to a demerit point system for errant conduct, like touting or soliciting street-hail jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As the profile of private hire car drivers is quite different from taxi drivers, the eligibility criteria for their respective licences will not be exactly the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As per current criteria, private hire car drivers must either be employed as a driver in a limousine company or be registered as an owner of a chauffeured services company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will only need to undergo a short briefing on the chauffeured services industry and regulations unique to the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will allow them to easily switch between taxi driving and providing chauffeured services using private hire cars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Singapore Taxi Academy will continue to be the training provider for the TDVL.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: LTA will later decide on who would provide the PDVL.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will also help to assure commuters that the vehicle is, indeed, registered with LTA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: LTA will make more detailed announcements later today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have taken a practical, balanced and minimalist approach in these new regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will ensure that we meet our key objectives of protecting commuters' interests and safety, allowing the point-to-point transport industry to continue to grow and innovate and also, at the same time, helping our taxi industry adjust to new and disruptive "sharing" technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 32 Let me now turn to the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) and Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) policy questions raised by Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about the next-generation ERP system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This new system will open up many opportunities to improve our transport system, beyond congestion management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There is, of course, potential to offer added-value services to motorists, such as using it to replace the paper coupon usage for roadside parking, getting more accurate and real-time traffic information, providing such real-time information to motorists and also including enhancements to the Off-Peak Car schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Perera also raised concerns about privacy under the next-generation ERP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For the purposes of traffic management, only aggregated data will be used by LTA and we will also ensure that the appropriate data security technologies and controls are put in place for all data use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MHA has already addressed the ERP 2.0 for security uses and I will not go further into that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Perera has made some good suggestions that MOT will also take on board to study as we look at the renewal of the ERP system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap shared his concern regarding COEs for motorcycles and suggested different forms to make the Cat D motorcycle COE framework better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested riding on the introduction of the next-generation ERP system to consider increasing COE quotas for motorcycles, on the basis that ,being smaller in size, they contribute less to congestion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, I would like to point out that the lesser contribution of motorcycles to congestion is already accounted for in the lower ERP rates they pay, compared to other vehicle types.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In addition, owners of motorcycles enjoy several concessions, such as lower taxes, compared to car owners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On the specific suggestion of allowing Cat D owners to have unlimited shorter-term renewal, currently, COE tenures are all fixed at 10 years for all categories and, as a concession, vehicle owners are allowed a five-year renewal on the condition that they deregister their vehicle thereafter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It can also lead to older and potentially more pollutive motorcycles remaining on our roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is a phenomenon that we actually see today, where older motorcycles are kept on the roads for a long time, polluting the air.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While these suggestions are on the table, we will continue to study this and see how we can make the Cat D framework better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But, ultimately, the COE system is designed to help control Singapore's vehicle population, given the land constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Minister Khaw has explained, there is very limited room for us to grow the overall vehicle population, whether it is for cars or motorcycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should, therefore, be very cautious about increasing the COE supply in one form or another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Instead, we should be encouraging Singaporeans to move towards public transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Having said that, I do know that COE is a hot topic and LTA does regularly review the COE framework to keep the system updated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested levying a COE surcharge on multiple COEs registered to a household.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Indeed, he pointed out that this is not a new suggestion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It would also inadvertently penalise households that are larger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: LTA had, therefore, decided not to Page: 33 implement such a measure back in 2013 after extensive consultation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: All the considerations and findings had been shared and discussed with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Yee Chia Hsing have offered suggestions to address the trend of Cat E COEs being used mainly to register Cat B cars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Cat E provides flexibility in the COE system by allowing the vehicle mix to evolve in response to market demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While most of the Cat E COEs in recent years have gone to Cat B, this has not been the case always.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For instance, Cat E COEs were routinely used to register Cat C vehicles between the years 2008 and 2010, when Cat C COE prices exceeded that of Cats A and B COE prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We also saw this in recent COE bidding exercises just this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are not keen on lowering the contribution rate to zero as it is still helpful to keep some fluidity within the system, so that COEs can still move across different categories to meet demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Again, the COE system, as I have said, is one area that LTA monitors closely and we will continue to study this area with all the suggestions that are given.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is because when an ETS-eligible vehicle is deregistered, that COE can be used to register a new vehicle within a one-month period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This means that the owner of the ETS-eligible vehicle would already have a COE obtained in this manner and would not need to bid for a fresh COE for his or her new vehicle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng also asked if we should consider smoothening the supply of Cats A and B COE quotas in the coming year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is really difficult to determine the optimal amount of quota supply to hold back and determine the right time to release the withheld quota back into the system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The risks of inadvertently causing even more volatility in COE premiums are very real.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In any case, even our projections were not right on target.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, we feel that it is better that we leave it to the market to determine the supply of quotas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To conclude, a car-lite Singapore does not mean a carless Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Car-lite is about creating an ecosystem of transport options in the form of good quality public transport, first-and-last-mile options and point-to-point services like taxis and chauffeured services, so that Singaporeans feel that their commuting needs can be met without owning a car.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Importantly, it also requires a change in mindset, lifestyle and culture to one of sustainable, smart and green mobility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Minister Khaw and Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo have stated, we have started the journey and, together, we ask Singaporeans to come along this journey with all of us to make our transportation system better and greener for the future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on what are the new capabilities that will be developed as part of these developments that can benefit and differentiate Singapore as a maritime and air hub and for businesses to look forward to?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, Singapore also saw the sale of its national liner, NOL, to a foreign entity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does the sale of NOL impact our position as a strategic maritime hub, given that a foreign entity now has better access to our strategic port facilities?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The redevelopment of our strategic plan and maritime capabilities would enhance our economic and transport standing in the region.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But it is also important that these developments provide for meaningful business and jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can we get young Singaporeans also excited about the prospects of working in these transport hubs, given that these are not typical professions that our young look forward to?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think there is that scope to make it sexier.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Budget airlines typically keep costs down by deploying the flight, cabin crew and aircraft in the most economically efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Furthermore, these low-cost carriers may get more red-eye flights, as well as less favourable arrival and departure timings, with short turnaround flights as well.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: By that, it may mean that the pilots have tight rosters and operate at or near maximum flight and duty time limits.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: As for the cabin crew, they may have to work extra hard to turnaround the plane within shorter timelines.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Staff should have sufficient rest periods during duty time to perform at an optimal level, so that neither service delivery nor the well-being of crew is compromised.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: With hectic working hours, safety and welfare conditions of the airline crew should be looked into.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Currently, there is little data or research done in this area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, our financial services, tourism, manufacturing and logistics sectors are Page: 35 considerably enhanced because of our position as aviation and maritime hubs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our air hub now provides good jobs to some 55,000 people.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The dedication and pride of these staff have made Changi Airport the most-awarded airport worldwide for passenger experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a result, passenger traffic has continued to grow.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Airfreight volumes, which have been lacklustre everywhere, still managed a 0.5% growth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We continue to be optimistic about Changi's prospects.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Air travel in the Asia Pacific is projected to double over the next two decades.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also put in place policies to ensure that Changi remains a leading air hub and continues to provide good global connectivity for our people and businesses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If Asia grows as projected, passenger traffic through Changi can also be expected to grow at between 3% and 4% annually over the next two decades.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A key plank of our strategy to ride this growth momentum is to expand Changi Airport.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Works to operationalise a three-runway system are also going well, with Changi Airport Group (CAG) having awarded the first construction contract in October 2015.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We expect the three-runway system to be operational in the early 2020s.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The centrepiece in positioning Changi Airport for the future is Terminal 5.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Since finalising its concept plan in 2014, we have been engaging the aviation community to develop a robust and flexible design that will stand the test of time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a mammoth task, as Members will know by now, that when T5 is fully developed, it will, in fact, be bigger than Terminals 1, 2 and 3 combined.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, you take Terminals 1, 2 and 3 today, put them together and imagine what Terminal 5 is going to be like.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With Terminals 1, 2 and 3 today, if you just add them up, it is 66 million passengers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After Jewel Changi Airport, actually Terminal 1 should be able to handle a little bit more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is the scale that we are talking about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will have to last us much longer than that, but around 2050, that is when you can have a major upgrade.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The architects for the design have a heavy responsibility; they will be appointed within the next one to two years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As was the case when we moved our airport from Paya Lebar to Changi, the expansion of our air hub will create many good jobs for Singaporeans and business opportunities for our companies, in areas ranging from airport management to aircraft maintenance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we are also mindful that with our manpower constraints, quantum improvements in productivity are needed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Efficiency-enhancing innovations must be incorporated into the new facilities at Changi as well as existing ones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These efforts will be complemented by programmes to attract Singaporeans to take up aviation careers and continuously upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The bottom line is this: for our air hub, we must always be ready to take advantage of improved technologies as they become available.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One aspect of aviation which requires constant and careful attention is safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of us do not have to think too much about it and that is only because many other people in aviation spend a great deal of time and resources to make sure that we get to fly safely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, I am glad that Mr Ang Hin Kee has asked about rest, welfare, training and other needs of low-cost carrier crew, Page: 36 because it is, ultimately, about safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All Singapore carriers, both full-service and low-cost carriers, are required to meet the same safety standards for fatigue management and crew training and competency promulgated by the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These standards are based on scientific research and studies and consistent with the requirements of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You have to set the standards and what are the standards based on?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And you have to leverage on other studies that are present, or do your own studies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of our airlines have done their own studies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In particular, there are mandatory rest periods between duty periods to ensure that the crew have sufficient rest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All airlines are also required to have structured training and competency frameworks and ensure that their crew maintain currency in their operational duties.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Tests are conducted annually to ensure that crew members have the necessary competencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Rules aside, it is penny-wise and pound-foolish for anyone involved in aviation to take chances with safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has very much to do with culture.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why in the Singapore air hub, we instil and reinforce a safety culture through stringent independent audits and regular exercises.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another area where safety matters a great deal is in air traffic management (ATM).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Members know, CAAS manages the airspace known as the Singapore Flight Information Region (FIR).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Singapore FIR, which was assigned by ICAO in 1946, has seen air traffic grow by leaps and bounds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But of this number, around 40% were over-flights, meaning that they neither landed at nor departed from Changi; they are just over-flights.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are part of the air connectivity of other countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the importance of the Singapore FIR to the international aviation community – it is not just for us, it is for the international aviation community – Singapore takes its responsibility as the FIR manager very seriously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To ensure the highest levels of safety and efficiency and to prepare for the growth in regional air traffic, CAAS invests heavily to enhance our ATM capabilities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our state-of-the-art ATM system – the third-generation Long Range Radar and Display System (LORADS III) – is one of the most advanced in the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We continually incorporate advanced technologies, such as Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B), which allows CAAS to extend tracking of aircraft beyond radar coverage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This, in turn, allows us to provide better ATM services to more aircraft to fly safely within a block of airspace.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From 2018, we expect to also use satellite technology to track aircraft.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within Southeast Asia, this is the only cluster of research and development focusing on ATM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In less than three years, the initiative has built up a pool of more than 50 researchers and funded more than 20 Page: 37 projects.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, CAAS is working with its counterparts in Thailand and Hong Kong to develop a concept to better manage air routes with heavy traffic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Typically, air traffic controllers worry about getting departing flights out on time, but not whether there could be bunching when these flights arrive at their destinations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, as an air traffic controller, if you have a job to get a flight out, your job is to make sure it gets out on time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But you never really worried about what happens when it arrives at the destination airport and if there could be bunching.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This collaboration will allow air traffic controllers at both the departure and arrival airports to share information and adjust the departure times of flights to avoid bunching at both ends.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is especially helpful for busy routes which will get more congested as regional air traffic grows; it will minimise delays and optimise capacity usage at each airport – and we know airport capacity is very expensive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We intend to pair up with more airports so we can manage the growing air traffic in our region more efficiently.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As all fair-minded users of our air navigation services can attest, CAAS air traffic controllers conduct their operations professionally and objectively, in accordance with international standards and best practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the help of technology and research insights, our controllers will raise their game and uphold the trust and confidence of the international aviation community using the Singapore FIR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On this note, let me reiterate that FIR boundaries are designated by ICAO based on technical and safety considerations to ensure air traffic safety and efficiency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Inevitably, FIRs cross national airspace boundaries and air traffic controllers are expected to consistently and professionally handle aircraft movements in their designated FIRs, irrespective of who owns the airlines, where the flights originate from or are headed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If FIR boundaries were based on state boundaries alone, we would see fragmentation of regional airspaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means breaking them up into smaller pieces with more parties managing the airspaces, more complexity, multiple points of coordination and, certainly, more safety risks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, fragmentation of regional airspaces runs counter to calls by the international aviation community, particularly the airlines which have to operate the flights, for more seamlessly-integrated airspaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Europe is taking the lead on this move, with the Single European Sky vision being one such example.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, with air traffic in ASEAN projected to grow strongly, it is all the more important that airspaces in our region be more integrated, not less.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We need to enable more aircraft to fly safely and efficiently within the same volume of airspace.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The shipping industry, which anchors our maritime sector, has been in difficult waters for several years now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the first time since the 2009 Global Financial Crisis, PSA saw container volumes decline last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Charter rates for offshore and dry bulk carriers have come under intense pressure due to weakened demand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Page: 38 Nevertheless, the medium- to longer-term outlook is positive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over the years, we have made significant gains in building up various aspects of our International Maritime Centre.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is today more multifaceted and vibrant than before, with activities ranging from maritime insurance to LNG bunkering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Moreover, the maritime community here is resilient and adaptable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With Government support, we believe that recovery in shipping will return and broad-based growth momentum will pick up again.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To lend a helping hand to shippers, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) enhanced the port dues concession to offshore support vessels in November last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last week, MPA extended the concession to dry bulk carriers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MPA has also granted an additional 10% port dues concession to container vessels calling at Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not a lot of money but I am told that they are nonetheless well appreciated by the industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In spite of the current headwinds, Singapore's International Maritime Centre continues to stay ahead of the competition.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For two years in a row, Singapore has topped the Baltic/Xinhua international shipping centre development index, which ranks the relative performance of maritime centres around the world.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, our port has just been voted "Best Seaport in Asia" for the 27th time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These accolades were not easy to come by and we do not take them for granted, even though we got it for the 27th time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are a result of careful nurturing of a robust maritime ecosystem that has taken many years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As in all business sectors, corporate restructurings are not uncommon.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The strength of our maritime cluster does not depend on whether the companies are Singapore-owned but whether they see value in being anchored here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For maritime businesses which can have very long investment horizons, the key is that our policies must be sound and consistent over time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked about the sale of NOL.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We all feel a bit "sayang" because it is like marrying off a daughter that has long been a flag-bearer of our maritime sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But at the same time, let us also recognise who the suitor is and the way the marriage could work out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The merged entity draws on the complementary strengths of both groups and provides a firmer footing for them to compete with the giants.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: NOL brings something to the table, CMA-CGM brings something to the table that the other party does not quite have.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a testament to Singapore's importance as a maritime hub and will reinforce Singapore's leadership position in container shipping.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Zaqy Mohamad pointed out, it is crucial that Singapore continues to enhance our value proposition as a maritime hub.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, we are taking proactive steps to develop the key capabilities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, we will continue to invest in building port capacity that meets the industry's long-term needs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Works on the Pasir Panjang Terminal are on schedule and reclamation works for the new Page: 39 Tuas Terminal are progressing well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Infrastructure aside, technology is an enabler to improve capabilities, as well as the quality of maritime jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are investing in technology as a multiplier of capacity, to boost productivity and transform current jobs into higher quality, higher value-added jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A good example can be found in PSA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In many ports, conventional rail-mounted gantry cranes are individually manned and operated from booths that sit atop each crane.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, PSA has introduced new systems at Pasir Panjang Terminal where a single crane specialist can remotely monitor and control the operations of several cranes, from the comfort of an air-conditioned control room.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Better comfort means better concentration and higher productivity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new Tuas Terminal will be a greenfield site that offers exciting opportunities for the use of smart technologies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, instead of prime mover drivers, driverless vehicles will ferry container boxes around our port.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will provide new job opportunities in engineering and software development.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Meanwhile, the next-generation Vessel Traffic Management System to be deployed at Tuas will need skilled data analysts and data scientists to predict congestion hotspots and to avoid potential collisions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To spur the development of a vibrant maritime technology cluster in Singapore, MPA has been actively encouraging R&D and innovation through the Maritime Innovation and Technology or MINT Fund.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One such organisation is the Energy Research Institute at NTU where a new Maritime Energy Test Bed facility was launched last November in collaboration with the Singapore Maritime Institute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This facility will help build up R&D capabilities in areas concerning ship emissions and abatement, alternative marine fuels and energy storage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The MINT Fund is also helping to put Singapore at the forefront of the global push towards cleaner marine fuels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Supported by the MINT Fund, Singapore company Billion Miles Pte Ltd is pioneering a methanol fuel blend system for marine engines to run on methanol.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The attractiveness of this system is that it requires only minor modifications to conventional bunkering infrastructure on top of vessels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Part of the MINT Fund's enhancements will be directed towards encouraging product and solution development for the maritime industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, with the support of the MINT Fund, local firm Hope Technik developed the Water Spider – a buoyant, waterproof drone that can be deployed to monitor oil spills or support search and rescue operations in Singapore's waters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The MINT Fund will support more of such technologies and use-inspired R&D to further promote maritime innovation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides harnessing cutting-edge technologies to our advantage, having a highly-skilled workforce sets us apart from our competitors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to invest in developing manpower for the maritime sector, especially during periods of slow growth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, help more Singaporeans know more about jobs and careers in the maritime sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I note Mr Zaqy Mohamad's point that we have to try and make it more "attractive and sexy", as he Page: 40 said.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, make sure that those who are interested gain the skills and experience to take on the job opportunities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And, third, support for those in the sector − upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the support of our unions and industry associations, we will do more to raise Singaporeans' awareness of good jobs and rewarding careers in the maritime sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, this is one of MPA's priorities for this year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, it is organising the inaugural Maritime Youth Festival, where outreach activities will help generate curiosity and interest about the maritime sector among our youths.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To complement these outreach efforts, the Singapore Maritime Foundation's Maritime Singapore Connect Office will intensify efforts to profile the maritime sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will provide a platform to connect employers, schools, relevant Government agencies, industry associations and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, it will develop an online portal to provide access to information and guidance on maritime careers and training opportunities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also equip Singaporeans with the necessary skills and experience to take advantage of job opportunities in the maritime sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The scheme will defray the costs incurred by employers when providing internship placements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One good example is Ms Ong Pei Wen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She shows how internships can help students kickstart their careers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She was a recipient of the MPA Global Internship Award while a student at NTU.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Her internship was at Shipowners' P&I Club and her host company was impressed by her good performance and attitude and offered her a job upon graduation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: GAP seeks to place University, Polytechnic and ITE graduates in participating maritime companies so as to help them gain industry experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise that companies are under pressure to cut costs amid this downturn.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, MPA will provide monthly stipends to graduates on the programme to encourage companies to take them on board, rather than turn them away.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of the many such individuals who have taken advantage is Mohammad Huzaifah bin Rasidi.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Huzaifah was previously a technician working at a shipyard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Peering out at sea from where he worked, he was amazed to see tug boats towing far larger vessels and oil rigs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In February last year, he took the plunge and joined the pioneer batch of trainees for the 15-month tug-master training programme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Huzaifah is now gearing up for his final examinations and looks forward to graduating this year as a tug-master, sometime in May.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MPA will announce the details of these new programmes shortly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In closing, Mdm Chair, Singapore and Singaporeans have benefited from our strengths as aviation and maritime hubs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are committed to enhancing Singapore's connectivity to the world by investing in first-class infrastructure and technologies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, we will develop a Page: 41 future-ready workforce that will uphold the standing of our twin hubs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because quite a lot of commuters have been complaining about the hot morning sun; it is very glaring.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just from the commuters in Khatib.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have also heard about this from commuters who use Yishun and other stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo said that MOT is already working with building owners to encourage them to build linkways to link up with Government-built linkways.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: But it is up to building owners to decide whether to build the linkways.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I suppose the Civil Service Club at Bukit Batok is a Government-owned building.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Will MOT encourage the Government to take a lead so that the rest of the building owners from the private sector will also follow?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For the second clarification, I agree with Senior Minister of State Ng Chee Meng that Cat E COEs, at times, are used for Cat C and Cat A vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: But the fact remains that the majority of the Cat E COEs, a big majority, are used for Cat B vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It also appears from the speech that MOT is not quite ready to do a reset of the COE distribution across the different categories.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, would Senior Minister of State Ng Chee Meng agree that it is not healthy for Cat B COE to continue to grow in this proportion, beyond 30%, or is it something that the Senior Minister of State would like to see increase beyond 50%?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Lastly, many industry players reckon that COE bidders, particularly the industry players, will likely be more careful in bidding for COEs if we adopt a pay-as-you-bid	system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It is not a new topic but I hope the Senior Minister of State would consider doing a trial in one of the categories; perhaps Cat A.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think it will be wonderful if the clarifications could be as short as the Minister's response, but I know it is a tall order.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you can meet it halfway, it would be fantastic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
